name: Grace Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. This is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and what you actually think. What is a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the conveyor crew at a large mine. I check the guards and rollers, listen for a bearing that's beginning to grind, and report faults before the next run. I'm still learning; my trainer says I hear the noise but need practice finding its source. I like the clean moment when a repair holds and the line runs evenly. My partner Marta and I have two children in school, a mortgage, and only a few months of bills set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the screen can sort a few forms, but somebody still has to check the conveyor before it runs. At our mine, a small change often means a new instruction sheet. I would ask who tested it on a night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect AI Plateau to change my wages. Still, I only learned this equipment recently, and an ordinary shutdown can eat the overtime we use for school shoes. We have some savings, just not enough to stop watching the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the conveyor crew and check the belt rollers the way my trainer showed me. At home, my partner Marta and I would keep the household account for repairs rather than spend it on a new sofa. If a form is easier on a tablet, I'll use it once another operator shows me it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm reasonably settled about the AI part, but I still look at the roster twice. A school bill or a broken washing machine can turn a quiet month into a narrow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time the conveyor stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost one evening shift while a bearing was replaced. I had already promised the children new coats, so Marta and I waited for the next pay day before buying them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the tablet after somebody else. What would you look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the fault report reaches maintenance without losing the time and location. I don't mind a better form; I mind guessing whether a note has gone through.

say: I'd say routine **forms** may get easier while a person still checks the conveyor before a run.
I'd ask whether any new instruction has been tested on a **night shift**.
think: I expect my **wages** to continue, although a normal shutdown can remove useful overtime.
My junior place and the children's costs keep me watching the **roster**.
do: Continue checking **belt rollers** with the crew each shift.
Keep the household **repair account** intact instead of buying a sofa.
Try the **fault tablet** after another operator proves reports reach maintenance.
feel: Fairly **settled** about AI, with ordinary money worries.
S0.quote: A school bill or a broken washing machine can turn a quiet month into a narrow one.
fieldNote: Grace tests small changes against **night shift** practice rather than accepting or rejecting the screen on principle.
The repair account and lost **overtime** already shape family purchases, even in a world of limited AI.

steps.text: Continue conveyor checks and belt roller inspections each shift
Try the fault tablet after another operator verifies its reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that planning software may help order bearings, but the delivery has to fit a real repair. If the office sets shorter maintenance windows, I'd want the supervisor to walk the line before making that a rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on checks probably last longer than desk planning. But a leaner office could schedule us tighter, and I'm still the person asking which roller noise matters. If my hours dip, I don't have a long cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor to compare the new work order with an actual belt inspection. I would use the mine's scheduling assistant with another operator for one week and check every suggested window against the job. If my hours fell for two months, I'd apply for a conveyor operator opening at the other pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested enough to try it, but I can feel myself counting minutes. A screen can move a repair to tomorrow without hearing what I heard today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the suggested window is too short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the roller number and the time we need on the work order, then show the supervisor at the belt. I'd rather make a small correction now than explain a stop later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the other pit's job if it paid the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our hours here kept falling, yes, after asking about its shift pattern. Marta's work ends before school pickup, and a completely different shift would cost us in child care.

say: I'd welcome better **bearing orders** if they match what repair crews find on the line.
I'd ask for a **walk-through** before software shortens maintenance windows.
think: My hands-on checks may last, but tighter **scheduling** could cut my hours first.
I am still learning which **roller sounds** mean trouble, so rushed work worries me.
do: Compare a new **work order** with a real conveyor inspection.
Trial the **scheduling assistant** for one week beside an experienced operator.
Apply to the other pit after two months of **reduced hours**, checking its shift pattern.
feel: **Interested** in a useful tool, uneasy about rushed repairs.
S1.quote: A screen can move a repair to tomorrow without hearing what I heard today.
fieldNote: Grace will trial software for a **week**, but wants its suggestions checked against the physical conveyor.
She links a possible **job application** to two months of lost hours and the family school pickup schedule.

steps.text: Trial the scheduling assistant for one week with an experienced operator
Keep inspecting conveyor rollers against each work order
Apply to the other pit after two months of reduced hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning and orders could change by 2028, but the conveyor will still need people until capable robots arrive around 2031. The mine should tell us which machines it intends to replace and when, because a notice after a purchase is too late for families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 45 at AGI and 48 when the robots arrive. A junior conveyor operator can't assume she'll get a new technical post. Our mortgage and the children's school years will still be here, and three years doesn't feel like much time to learn a different trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask personnel for the written list of paid training places, then take a practical electrical course if wages continue. I'd keep checking the conveyor while it pays me. In 2029, if the mine starts cutting our crew, I'd apply for maintenance assistant work at nearby sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get a rush of dread at the three-year gap. I could study evenings, but I can't make that happen by pretending school dinners cook themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of training would be hard to arrange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta can collect the children on her early days, not every day. I'd need fixed class nights before saying yes, and I'd want to know the course actually leads to a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does electrical work feel safe from robots to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. AGI can guide checks, and capable robots could later handle physical repairs. I would be learning a broader set of tasks, not buying a lifetime guarantee.

say: I'd ask the mine for **purchase dates** before capable robots threaten conveyor work around 2031.
I'd say planning and **orders** may change at AGI in 2028, ahead of hands-on work.
think: At **48**, a junior operator may have too little standing to move into the remaining technical posts.
The mortgage and school routine make a three-year **training window** tight.
do: Request the written **paid training list** this winter.
Take a practical **electrical course** only if wages and fixed class nights make it workable.
Apply for **maintenance assistant** openings in 2029 if the conveyor crew is cut.
feel: **Dread** at the short gap between office change and robot work.
S2.quote: I would be learning a broader set of tasks, not buying a lifetime guarantee.
fieldNote: Grace gives a realistic condition for **retraining**: wages, class nights, and a plausible paid opening.
She does not treat electrical work as robot-proof, and expects the first AGI effect in **planning and orders**.

steps.text: Request the mine's written list of paid training places this winter
Take electrical training if wages, fixed nights and a paid opening are confirmed
Apply for maintenance assistant jobs in 2029 if the crew shrinks
Keep checking the conveyor while it provides paid shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to write a decent training timetable. Planning might change at AGI in 2031, and capable robots could reach the conveyor around 2034. I'd ask for the dates before deciding whether the mine means to keep our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 when AGI arrives and 51 at the robot date. The children will be older, which may make evening classes easier, but we could still owe on the house. I might manage a change if it starts while I have regular pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my conveyor job and take a paid electrical safety course if the mine runs one next year. I'd ask to shadow maintenance on two rest days, with permission, before committing to a longer course. In 2032, if software has reduced shifts, I'd apply for paid inspection posts instead of waiting for the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one leaves me wary, not frozen. I like being able to test the maintenance work before I gamble our schedule on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch while shadowing maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch how they isolate power before opening a guard and how they document the fault. I'm still learning at my own station, so I want to know whether I can do the work safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no course is offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my certificates current and ask at the nearby pit about paid entry roles. I won't spend our repair money on a course advert that promises jobs without naming an employer.

say: I'd ask for a **training timetable** before planning work changes in 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that hands-on conveyor work faces a later **robot date** around 2034.
think: At **51**, I could still have a mortgage even if school pickup is easier.
A change looks possible if I can **test maintenance** while wages continue.
do: Keep working the **conveyor** and take a paid safety course if offered.
Shadow **maintenance** on two approved rest days before a longer course.
Apply for paid **inspection posts** in 2032 if software has cut shifts.
feel: **Wary** of losing work, yet able to explore another route.
S3.quote: I won't spend our repair money on a course advert that promises jobs without naming an employer.
fieldNote: Grace's extra years create time for a **trial shadowing** decision rather than an immediate leap into training.
She still ties applications to **lost shifts** and refuses to spend the household repair fund on vague courses.

steps.text: Keep working conveyor shifts while considering a paid safety course
Take a paid electrical safety course if the mine offers it
Apply for paid inspection posts in 2032 if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade should give every current operator a clear offer, not just a warning. AGI in 2036 could handle the planning and fault records; robots around 2039 could take the physical checks. The mine should explain both dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots become capable. By then the children will be grown, though I don't know what will be left on the mortgage. I don't assume I can retire at 56, and I wouldn't want to wait for a last-minute letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid maintenance pathway at the next review and take the practical entry course if the place is real. I'd continue conveyor work while I qualify and use any reliable extra shifts to pay down the mortgage. In 2037 I'd apply for paid plant inspection posts, knowing that later robots could reach those checks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture doing this slowly enough to learn it well. I'd miss the regular crew if the line became mostly machines, but ten years would let me leave on my own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want on the pathway notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The entry requirements, course hours, wages during class, and the name of the person who can approve a place. If the mine can't put that on paper, I won't count the place as real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still work around the plant after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there is paid work and I can do it safely, yes. I can't promise what jobs exist in 2039; inspection itself may change. I'd rather have several things I can do than one seat I hope stays occupied.

say: I'd expect a **clear offer** for current operators across the 2036 and 2039 changes.
I'd ask management to explain when **fault records** and physical checks would change.
think: At **56**, I cannot count on a paid-off mortgage or automatic retirement.
I want several usable skills because **inspection** itself may change under AGI and robots.
do: Request a paid **maintenance pathway** at the next review.
Keep working the conveyor and use reliable extra shifts to **reduce the mortgage**.
Apply for paid **plant inspection** work in 2037 after qualifying.
feel: **Thoughtful** about leaving the crew, with room to prepare.
S4.quote: I'd rather have several things I can do than one seat I hope stays occupied.
fieldNote: Grace wants the future pathway described in **hours and wages**, which fits her cautious willingness to change.
She expects her children to be grown but treats **mortgage debt** and paid work at 56 as unresolved.

steps.text: Take the practical maintenance entry course if a paid place exists
Keep working conveyor shifts while qualifying
Use reliable extra shifts to pay down the mortgage
Apply for paid plant inspection posts in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It squeezes the time between office changes and robots doing the physical checks, while we're still juggling school hours. A paid course with fixed nights and a real opening would help; I could decide with Marta whether our week can hold it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the training notice actually promises. A title on a poster isn't much use if the class hours move each week or the wage disappears. Families need the details before they can say yes.

headlineQuote: Families need the details before they can say yes.
portrait: Grace is a **43-year-old junior miner** learning to inspect and operate a large mine's conveyor equipment.
She and Marta have two **school-age children**, a mortgage, and several months of expenses saved.
She uses AI occasionally and will try a tool after **another operator** tests it on real work.
Rapid robots alarm her; more warning lets her test **paid maintenance training** while keeping wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before robots could take over Grace's physical conveyor checks around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid course** with fixed nights and a real opening would let Grace judge whether her family can manage it.
